description: We are a team of engineers with backgrounds in mechatronics, renewable energy, and agritech. We focus on leveraging space data to solve Earth's pressing challenges—specifically designing innovative satellite-based solutions for smart disaster response (like wildfire suppression) and sustainable resource management.
summary:
Flame in Freefall turns NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) combustion
experiment archive into an explorable fire-safety tool for future Moon and
Mars habitats. It ranks 24 microgravity combustion investigations by how
closely their tested conditions (oxygen level, pressure, air flow) match a
habitat cabin, with every score broken down into its components so the
ranking stays explainable. A browser-side regression model, trained on the
FLEX droplet-combustion dataset with group-held-out cross-validation, lets
users explore how fuel, diluent, oxygen, pressure and droplet size affect
burn rate in real time. A material risk index estimates relative flammability
across 11 habitat materials, with every component explicitly labeled as
data-driven or literature-derived. Four data-backed insight cards translate
statistical findings into equipment-design implications, and a local Q&A
assistant answers visitor questions strictly from the site's own cited
sources. The project runs locally with a single command and is built
entirely on real, DOI-cited NASA data, with its limitations stated openly
throughout.
details:
What it does and how it works
Flame in Freefall is a locally run web application that turns 24 NASA PSI combustion investigations into one tool for judging fire risk in a habitat. It has four screens:

Explore ranks all 24 investigations by a transparent habitat-relevance score. The score combines O₂-range overlap (25%), pressure overlap (20%), low-flow overlap (15%), microgravity flight data (15%), data volume (15%) and solid-material presence (10%). The reference habitat is 17–35% O₂, 56–101 kPa and 0–20 cm/s flow. Each investigation shows its condition envelope, its score rationale, its DOI and a summary. A component with no data is shown as unknown, and investigations with too few known components are not scored.

Scenario predicts the droplet burn rate (K, mm²/s) for a chosen fuel/diluent pair, O₂ fraction, pressure and droplet diameter. The model is a Ridge regression trained on FLEX (PSI-69): 258 modeled tests out of 274 recorded, in 6 fuel×diluent groups. In cross-validation, each group is predicted without seeing any of its own tests (R² = 0.373, MAE = 0.087 mm²/s). Next to it, a flammability risk panel covers 11 habitat materials.

Equipment shows four statistically derived findings as cards. Each card has its sample size, a caveat and the DOI of its source.

FlameSense presents our concept for a pre-fire detection sensor box. It is clearly labeled “concept, not built.”

An AI assistant answers questions in plain language. A local Python server collects the relevant parts of the site’s own data and sends only those to an LLM, so every answer stays grounded in NASA data. If no model is available, the server answers with the closest finding cards instead.

Benefits and intended impact
Fire is one of the most serious hazards in long-duration space habitats. Decades of NASA combustion research already exist, but the results are spread across dozens of separate studies. Our tool brings that research into one place that is easy to explore and honest about its limits. Mission planners, habitat designers and researchers can use it to find the experiments that matter most for a given cabin atmosphere. They can also use it to reason about how materials burn in non-standard atmospheres such as reduced pressure and elevated oxygen.

Tools, languages and hardware

Data and modeling: Python (pandas, scikit-learn, DuckDB).

Frontend: vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS, in English and Turkish.

Server and AI: a Python standard-library HTTP server with an LLM through an OpenAI-compatible API. Nothing depends on external hosting.

Hardware concept: FlameSense was designed in Blender as a 140 × 90 × 45 mm enclosure. It holds an ESP32-S3 and six sensors: O₂, CO, CO₂, hot-wire flow, particulate and a thermal array.

How it is creative
We do not present NASA’s archive as a static list. Every dataset is read through a single practical question: is this relevant to keeping a habitat crew safe from fire? The design also separates what the data supports from what comes from assumptions or the literature. In the risk panel, for example, only PMMA’s threshold comes from flight data; the other ten materials are labeled as literature values.

Factors our team considered

Traceability: every number points to a specific NASA dataset and DOI.

Missing data: missing values are reported as missing and never filled with zero.

No data leakage: measurements taken after a test, such as burn time and extinction diameter, are excluded from the model’s inputs.

Honest validation: cross-validation keeps whole fuel×diluent groups out of training, which is stricter than a random split.

Clear limits: predictions are offered only for fuel/diluent pairs present in the data. No partial-gravity (Moon/Mars) data exists, so relevance scores reflect cabin-atmosphere overlap only.
